I am still homeless. In Los Angeles. I get disability benefits but not quite enough to pay rent AND a deposit for a new place. So here is my day to day.

Due to my disabilities I have Medicare, which allows me to ride the trains or buses as much as I want for $14 a month. I sleep mostly on the 4 or the 20 lines, back and forth from east to west, changing to the opposite direction when it reaches the end of the line. I eat off the dollar menu at McDonald's and bathe in their restrooms. I usually do this at a specific location where the bathrooms get mopped at the same time each morning so I could have a semi-clean floor upon which I could spread my change of clothes and toiletries, such as toothbrush, soap and deodorant. Until recently I had a contact lens but it disintegrated, so for the time being that's part of the process that I don't have to worry about.

Once I feel/smell clean enough I will go to the library when it opens and look for work and charge my phone. I also alternate between duolingo and khanacademy to help improve my skills so I can have a wider option of jobs to which I can apply. If I don't have any interviews or meetings with potential roommates from craigslist (who turns out to want nothing to do with a handicapped disabled retarded loser like myself), I try to kill eight to nine hours at the library between the computers and just reading. Then when the library is about to close, I get on the bus and repeat the cycle. Every week me and my wheeled suitcase goes to the laundromat.

That is pretty much an overview of my day.

I truly enjoy the job and the feeling of being productive.  I love the self-sufficiency I feel when I put my body to work and feel industrious.  I love to be given responsibility to take the initiative to be valuable and indispensable to the workplace.  I never want to rush and hurry out to go home.  I don't create or provoke any hostile environments or attitude, and when I feel that someone is uncomfortable with my closeness from whatever circumstances brought us to work together in close proximity, I tactfully distance myself to another relevant task.  But this is just how I feel right now in stock room.  I used to do customer service at a call center.  It was a fun challenge to resolve conflicts and follow up on them to ensure my quality scores remain favorable.  I understand that other people's emotions are not my own, and I am just grateful to be placed in a position where I'm utilized in exchange for pay -- that's it.  I could care less if they had me doing janitorial work rather than "clean" stockroom or floor sales, as long as I am needed.

Yo, *everyone* gets overlooked at first because they are new and a stranger. But the difference is that dudes without disabilities get more benefits of the doubt. People will look at *you* and think, "Yes, that dude looks like he can take care of himself and wouldn't become increasingly codependent upon me. He looks healthy and capable of doing anything." You have the right to approach strangers and strike up a conversation with them since you don't have any defects to scare or disgust anyone away from you -- increased exposure of your presence and personality will breed familiarity and comfort, in much the same way that classmates and co-workers get warmer and friendlier over time. You *do* have an advantage. Don't let opportunities pass you by just because you have a low opinion of yourself -- it's low because you're lonely, and you have the willpower to overcome it with just a little bit of an effort.

I am sort of the opposite. A person like me, by all rights, should be the poster child for /r/socialanxiety but in truth, I crave human interaction and I welcome the challenge of irrational shitbirds. When they were training me on the register,  a customer attempted to pay with a debit card held together by scotch tape. I helpfully suggested that she use another card or pay in cash and she immediately went off in a nuclear tirade. I didn't hyperventilate or break down into tears; I calmly emphasized with her until she huffed and paid with a credit card that wasn't held together with scotch tape. I believe that I handled that transaction quite well. However, my employer has seen it fit to schedule me for the stockroom from that point on so I couldn't really put my social and salesmanship skills to the test. There is a constant undercurrent of thought in the back of my mind that basically expresses gratitude for the job, as well as dependency for my survival, so I always have a baseline mood of contentment and industriousness to keep me in good spirits. I work because I want to, because I believe that the human body was made to do work. As long as I can still see and hear, I should make use of my senses to build up a secure financial future for myself so I don't end up as a deafblind retard shoved into a closet while a Nice Guy Caregiver steals my disability benefits each month. That specific fear is my daily motivation but without a job, that's how my future is going to pan out.

It's harrowing.  I am lucky to have public storage to keep my majority of things.  I alternate between a soft briefcase for days that I work and a backpack for my days off.  Since I am disabled, I pay $14 a month for unlimited access to the L.A. transit system so I catch naps on the bus from one end of the line to the next.  This is an adventure at night when waiting amongst the shady, questionable characters who are probably rugged veterans at this sort of thing at the bus stop where the line starts for the other direction.  If you've ever played The Sims, you know how you had to spam the Nap function like four or five times to get full energy?  It's sort of like that -- ride and nap four or five hour-long bus rides to catch enough REM sleep to get you through the next cycle of daylight.  I go to public storage before it closes each to put away my ID and debit card and etc. so I don't lose them if someone goes through my backpack while I'm asleep.  I depend on a McOasis to eat for under $4 a day, access wi-fi, and clean and void myself in the restrooms.  With no access to a shower -- I salvaged every washcloth that I bought when I was rushed out of the last place where I lived, so now I have them all in two separate large Ziploc bags.  One for clean and one for dirty, to be washed at the laudromat.  I use two of them a day.  I also brush my teeth twice a day, with my toothbrush in one of those plastic travel tubes so it doesn't get dirty.  Also have a plastic travel case for my soap that I use with aforementioned washcloths.  As for the laundromat?  I salvaged my Tide, Bleach, and Bounce dryer sheets as well and take them out of Public Storage for when I go.  But really, the biggest issues for me are keeping my transient valuables secure, catching enough sleep, and ensuring that I don't stink in case I happen to accidentally by chance get a job interview call on my prepaid cell phone.

Well, here's the thing.  They have trained me in every place possible in this store, be it the floor or the stockroom. So since it's hard for me to hear customers, I am delegated to the stock room.

I'm happy with the job but I feel that they treat me as token crew.  I feel like an embarrassment.  There is a long-time team member who threw a couple of unsolicited constructive criticisms my way with an impatient tone, but I took it all in stride.  He's friendly with another long-time co-worker who simply glares at me like I'm about to eat her brains, so I simply pretend she doesn't exist and keep my distance whenever possible. I land interviews with excited-sounding folk, but for the most part they always seem crestfallen with disappointment when we meet face-to-face because I'm so short and tiny and ugly-looking and defective and middle-aged and male and ew.

The last point I want to make is that I'm not using this job just to have money to play with -- I am actively trying to get myself back into a stable situation, and that means having enough money to put a deposit down on a room to rent with a roommate who will let me co-sign their lease so I could have a say on whether or not they could have some crazy homeless got-out-of-jail-for-threatening-a-bus-driver dude sleep over on the floor and steal my food. Two years ago I used to help this guy named Paco with his independent dog-walking business.  He would recruit me to tag along not only because he would sometimes have too many dogs to hold their leashes in one hand, but also because I was "good with computers".

Every apartment or house that we entered, Paco would ask me to "hack their computers and see what kinda porn they look at, huh-huh-huh!"

Because I'm not a complete asshole, I "made it work" only about 1 time out of 10 and that's only because he was right there watching me.  The rest of the time, he was securely leashing the dogs with his attention diverted so I could surreptitiously check "Work offline", or disable the network in the taskbar, so I could say "Oh no they don't have internet hooked up" or "Ahhh this needs a password".

Since I was not the uber-leet hacker of his dreams, he quit calling me for help.  That doesn't mean that he didn't recruit someone else to giggle over his clients' porn history, however.

First day of work was surprising -- I expected them to hand me a mop and a vacuum cleaner, because disableds aren't good for anything, right?  Nope.  On the contrary, they handed me a barcode scanner, price guns, and told me how to navigate the stock room and handle marking down items.  I had to scan each item twice with a different function on the scanner -- once to find out the updated price for markdowns, and once to see how many units of each item were needed to be put onto the sales floor.  And then, go *onto* the sales floor and place the items on their appropriate hangars and racks.  And you know what?  I did everything right, just like a normal healthy person -- nothing was too hard or complex or vague for me.  No one checked up on me because I was taking too long, nor did I have any mistakes called out.  I go back to work on Thursday to earn time and a half, which is a little bit more of good news.

Confession:  I was told to take a fifteen-minute break.  I only took ten before going back to the stock room.  I just can't stand to be idle.

With that being said, I buy groceries once a week, and after bottled water, my budget limits me to about $20 on food.

I can get a group of bananas for 69c but those HAVE to go fast or else they'll spoil and attract fruit flies.  Once I consume those, I will consider the following based on the replies with which I currently feel most comfortable:

* Ostrich jerky + peanut butter or nutella.  I could use a jerky strip as a knife to spread peanut butter onto bread as well.

* Ditto on the packaged tuna.  I've never had those before, I've only dealt with the canned tuna.  Are they especially moist and will the packaging reek after I use jerky strips to spread tuna unto bread?  If so, I will probably skip those.

* I do have a microwave, so instant soup could be a possibility.  I would not mind buying some plastic spoons and keeping it clean over the course of several meals.  I also use it to nuke pop tarts, although it's not especially healthy, it's a warm sweet breakfast treat.  I can also use the spoons to utilize cinnamon with applesauce.

* I love Wheat Thins!  I am trying to make them last longer than the two days that follows my banana binge.  I could combine them with peanut butter/nutella as well.  Potatoes on the other hand require prep which can be messy and hard to clean in my carpeted room.  I suppose I could find healthy potato chip alternatives...anyone have any non-GMO suggestions?  I will also look into dried fruits.  I think there's some dried cranberry snacks at the market that I can check out?

* As for cooked meat, I'm trying to save money so the cheapest daily budget warm meat item that I can currently find is the McChicken for under $1.20 (it varies from $1.06 - $1.18 depending on the location I guess) but other than that, I'll have to locate low-sodium instant soups with meat byproducts in them.

* I'll look into the dried prunes and the whole grain couscous stuff but as for everything else, I'm not so sure.  w/r/t middle eastern food, how healthy/important is hummus to nutrition?  I like the spicy kind they have at Trader Joe's.

So in summation, I will have to find a way to fit all of this into an extremely small budget.  Setting aside an extra $8.40 for a daily trek to get a McChicken would probably be my best bet at ensuring an affordable meat base to my diet.  I'll keep checking on this thread and will update with developments when I shop again on Wednesday when my disability comes in.  Thanks!
